lecture_metadata.title: But what is a neural network? (3Blue1Brown)

chunk_summaries: we show you what a neural network actually is, assuming no background, and to help visualize what it's doing, not as a buzzword but as an abstract piece of math . we're going to put together a video that focuses on the structure component of learning . the video is going to be devoted to the structure aspect of learning, and the following one will tackle the structure part of that . if you've been living under a rock, you probably haven't heard of it before .

we're going to put together a neural network that can learn to recognize handwritten digits . in this introductory video we'll look at the simplest plain vanilla form with no added frills and show you how it does fall short of a couple hopes that we might have for it . the network starts with a bunch of neurons corresponding to each of the 28x28 pixels of the input image . each one of these holds a number that represents the grayscale value of the corresponding digit .

we show you how a network of neurons can be trained to recognize digits based on a set of activations . the network is a neural network that is essentially a digit recognition network . we show how the network can be used to train the network to recognize the digit of a given digit . if you look at the network as an information processing mechanism, you'll see that the network has already been trained .

we show how a layered network can be trained to recognize digits if it feeds in an image with a loop up top and a line on the right . in a perfect world, we might hope that any generally loopy pattern towards the top sets off a particular neuron whose activation is going to be close to 1 . if you feed in an pixel image with an 8 or a 9 or an 8, there's a specific neuron in the second to last layer that corresponds to that digit . we'll show you how to train a network to recognize the digit in the third layer .

we show how to train a neural network to recognize the various little edges that make up a loop . the network can also be used to learn which subcomponents correspond to which digits . we also show how this can be used for other tasks that break down into layers of abstraction . this is a hope that we might have, a goal with the layered structure like this .

we're going to compute the weighted sum of all the pixel values associated with each of the connections between our neuron and the neurons from the first layer . we'll use green pixels to indicate positive weights, and red pixels for negative weights . if we make the weights associated with almost all of the pixels zero except for some positive values in this region that we care about, then we can compute their weight sum according to these weights in a little grid of their own .

we compute a weighted sum of all the pixel values in the region that we care about . the sum is largest when those middle pixels are bright but the surrounding pixels are darker . a common function that does this is called the sigmoid function that squishes the real number line into the range between 0 and 1, and it just steadily increases around the input 0. So the neuron in this network is basically a measure of how positive the relevant weight sum is .

we show you how to tweak the weights and biases of a neural network to make it behave in different ways . we show how to do this by tweaking the numbers so that the second layer picks up on edges and the third layer gets to pick up on patterns . this is a fun experiment that is at once fun and kind of horrifying . if you've built up a little bit of relationship with what those numbers actually mean, you have a starting place for learning .

we show you a more notationally compact way that these connections are represented . if you choose to read up more about neural networks, this is how you'd see it . we organize all of the activations from one layer into a column as a vector, and then organize all the weights as matrixes, where each row corresponds to the connections between one layer and a particular neuron in the next layer .

the sigmoid squishification function is a function that takes in the outputs of all the neurons in the previous layer and spits out a number between 0 and 1 . it's an absurdly complicated function that involves 13,000 parameters in the form of these weights and biases that pick up on certain patterns . if it were any simpler, what hope would we have that it could take on the challenge of recognizing digits? and how does it take on that challenge?

we'll show you a little bit more about this particular network that we're seeing is really doing . the network that underlies YouTube's recommendation algorithm is primed to believe that you want to see content from this channel get recommended to you . I'll also dig a bit deeper into what this network is actually doing and why it's doing it .

a max of zero and a where a is given by what you were explaining in the video . it's kind of motivated from a biological analogy with how neurons would either be activated or not so it would be zero so it'd be zero if it passes a certain threshold . a lot of people just tried ReLU and it happened to work very well for these incredibly deep neural networks .

lecture_metadata.title: Neoliberalism and the End of History - Part 3

chunk_summaries: MIT OpenCourseWare provides high-quality educational resources for free . to make a donation, or to view additional materials from hundreds of MIT courses, visit ocw.mit.edu . if you want to donate to a MIT course, please click here .

we look at the neoliberal policies of the last generation, which have simply undermined a very large part of the population . in 2007-- that's right before the crash, there was great euphoria among economists and intellectuals about the wonderful economy that we have today . a lot of it is a reaction to the policies that have undermined the population of the past generation . but it's also a response to the economic policies that we've seen in the past few years . we're going to be a long time .

a sociologist from the university of california tries to understand the paradox that the people who are suffering the most from these neoliberal policies are the ones who most support them . the more he kicks them in the face at every opportunity, the more they support him . I think it's very striking when you look at the last election, in fact . a woman who went to live in a very-red county in Mississippi went and integrated herself into society . she got to know the people in the bayou area of Mississippi .

we're all standing in a line. Behind us are our parents and our grandparents. They worked hard. They did everything the right way. They had families. They were religious. They're conservative. They have families. But all of a sudden, the line stalled. We've stopped. The problem is the people behind us. I mean, this is the way people see the world that way. And you can understand why they see it that way . i think the problem is that these people are being pushed by the federal government in front of us with affirmative action programs .

we're going to see a lot of scapegoating from the federal government if we turn our attention to somebody who's doing that to them . it's going to be a really ugly period unless there's a strong reaction, not after it takes place . we have plenty of examples in our own history, like the Nazis for example, and we've seen many examples of race riots back in our history . if you look at that amalgam and you can see why these people hate the government , you see how the government is keeping us alive .

we look at gynecology, which was developed by professors at Harvard Medical School . it's a subject that was good subjects . if you shoot any creole phonemic pattern in your French, then you're discarded . I think that's also true in the US . in the u.s., we have a one-drop rule .

in the case of Rachel Jeantel, who was a star witness in the trial of Zimmerman, she was discarded by the jury because she spoke with a black English accent . a linguist at Stanford, John Rickford, wrote a beautiful piece showing how because of the way she spoke, what she said was given no credibility . and this is why I think that perhaps one could think of race alongside language as a tool that you can use to create this illusion of hierarchies .

the picking up of a fake acc-- it shows up in many strange ways at MIT . in the early 1950s, there was a wave of Anglophilia . and people-- men, of course. No women-- dressed in English clothes and affected British accents . but these things happen all the time . they can be very pernicious when it's a part of the population that's vulnerable and deprived and under external pressures for other reasons .

lecture_metadata.title: Why Having More Doesn't Make You Happier (Science of Well-Being)

chunk_summaries: we're going to talk about the ebinghouse illusion when we think about those orange circles in the center . the orange circle on the right is exactly the same size as you can see when I get rid of the circles . because of the presence of these other circles on the outside, these other reference point blue circles, we actually don't see the circles at the exact same size, we can only see them relative to each other . if we look at a reference point, we think, "Whoa, that orange circle must be super big because all the blue circles around it are so small"

we're constantly judging relative to other stuff out there in the world and it messes up our judgment of what the thing we really care about our particular decision or particular circle, what size, what magnitude, what awesomeness it really is . a lot of people see these kinds of reference points messing up their happiness judgments . one of the most famous examples of this is Michael Phelps with one of his bazillions of gold medals that he won in 2008 .

we look at the expression of the guy who won the silver medal who is not as happy as Michael Phelps . if you're LLO and you were one second away from winning silver, what's your most salient reference point for other people's happiness? if it could have been like I was like one second from winning gold, what would have been your most important reference point if I had won silver? i think it's a good idea to look at it from a different perspective . we're looking at a lot of different perspectives .

a new study shows that the silver medal winners are actually way less happy than the bronze medal winners . it's not your absolute level or the absolute medal you got. It's what you think you could have gotten . if you're a bronze, what's your most salient reference point? a gold medal is a silver medal . the white bars are silver medals and the yellow bars are bronze guys . that's kind of a reference point in action .

we've seen that most of our evaluation of what a good job is actually concerned with having a high salary . that's for better or for worse what everybody seems to care about . what we see in terms of our own reference point is what was happening to us in the past or what we're doing right now that seem to mess us up in just the same way . if you're making $30,000 and you think about your next raise, you say, "Well, the required income I would need to be happy is 50K"

two economists did a nice analysis of what's the jumping point . they found that for every amount that your actual income goes up a dollar, your required income, the income you think you want, actually goes up $140 . and this happens at every raise point, if I survey you, you actually think you're not making enough. You want to make more . the more annoying reference point that messes us up even more is not our own current status is messing up what we think the good status is .

we look at how social comparison affects whether or not we like our salary, but also like our job . we find that a person's job satisfaction actually goes down as their comparative income goes up . if you're in a place where your co-workers have a higher salary than you, you like your job even less . this is what psychologists call social comparison . it's the act of evaluating yourself relative to other people .

a new study by snick and hemingway shows that if you're in a job where your co-workers have a higher salary than you, you are just necessarily less happy with your job . over 50% of people choose having half of the income so they won't be less than others, which is pretty crazy . uh, this also explains some of the reasons why earning less than other people causes so much hardship .

we look at how much worse are you than if you had a job across different cities in the UK with different unemployment rates . we find a nice negative relationship between the well-being of people who are unemployed and those who are employed . if the overall job rate around you is really bad, it's not as bad for you as if it were in a spot where lots of other people are not unemployed . so to test this, we looked at a study that looked at whether or not people who were unemployed are fine .

we look at what counts as a reasonable social comparison for people who are employed or in their zip code . we find that if you're employed in a spot where lots of other people are unemployed, it's not as bad for you even though all the people around you are ne are not having the income they might expect . if we take in these reference points that are kind of crazy, we take them in as reference points . this is a great example of how to use these references to make a good social comparison .

people who watch a lot of TV are faced with people with crazy salaries, crazy incomes, crazy beauty levels, crazy stuff . does that make you less satisfied with your own salary, does that mess up your intuitions about what normal salaries around you are? if you go up in numbers of hours of TV watching, you also go down in your estimate of your own wealth relative to others . the more TV you watch, the more unhappy you are with your income . and what do you do to keep up with the Joneses?

we find that for every hour of extra TV watching you we you do a week you are spending on average $4 more each week in household spending . we also find that people who live close to people who have won the lottery are buying new cars . if you live in a neighborhood where you have a prominent new car sitting in your garage, does that mess with you? if so, do you want to buy your own awesome new car even though you didn't win the lottery and you can't afford it?

we talk about how people who win the lottery are almost twice as likely to buy a new car themselves if they live next to a person who won the lottery than if you're just kind of in a control case . a lot of people in control cases don't like to buy cars at a certain rate . we also talk about what happens in the context of good grades . this is a really insidious reference point .

we're going to show you a cool study by Brerle and Megan to see how spiteful students might be about other people's grades . they did an experiment in their own classes to see what kind of behavior they might exhibit . if you check this off, your final grade point average is going to go up by a half a point, which sounds awesome . but you know, because it's 0.5, not everybody's going to get the benefit of this .

we found that about 41% of students rejected the proposal to do this . the rejections were higher in the top 50% of the class than across the board . in fact, they were about 10% higher than across all the classes . a lot of the students rejected it .

we look at how social comparisons can mess up our happiness and our mood . we find that when you look at pictures of models and magazines, you get about a 2.3 on a four-point happiness scale before and after looking at magazines and magazines . if you're like me at an airport or at a news stand looking at all these things, we're constantly faced with these comparisons that don't match with what the average is . this is a spot that's super insidious . it's a big part of the problem is that we can't really fix it .

we look at how social comparisons are messing up our perceptions of ourselves and other people around us . if you look at pictures of other people who might happen to be hotter than your spouse, does that mess up your absolute rating of your spouse? a study by um Kendrick in a different paper looked at this too . we found that a few minutes of looking at these kinds of pictures makes you more unhappy . this is a small difference, but it shows you that we face a particular set of reference points messing us up .

we look at how much looking at your social comparisons on Facebook improves or messes up your self-esteem after you've looked at Facebook . we find that there's a pretty high correlation between Facebook use and self esteem . if you're on Facebook and on Snapchat, are you looking to see like are other people like having a really bad day? or are you on Snapchat like, "Whoa, everybody else's Saturday night is way better than mine?"

a new study shows that the more Facebook use you have, the lower your self-esteem . the correlation between income and happiness is about 0.1 . but unlike the other correlation, this correlation is in the negative direction . if you're making downward comparisons with the loserish people, your self esteem is about that . so you can't say did it work? if it didn't work, it worked .

rated self-esteem is about that on a fivepoint scale . uh I'm plotting kind of these big ratings of yourself and other people . these white bars are yourself when you're making upward and downward social comparisons . the weird thing is you don't get that same bump for yourself if you look at the losery people, you might think you bump up your own perception of yourself .

this annoying feature that our mind doesn't think in terms of absolutes. It thinks relative to reference points . it just soaks in whatever reference point we get . and so, the more you can kind of force that filter on it, the better you will be .
